summary: Heartbeat overtaking final payload suppresses concluding paragraph on multiplexed SSE sessions
description:
Issue summary: Several NotePulse customers observed SSE chat sessions where the server`s heartbeat frames sometimes arrive between the final chunk and the explicit end-marker; when the client library treats heartbeat as higher-priority multiplex traffic the final paragraph (closing punctuation + metadata) is not surfaced to the application and the stream ends without the concluding chunk.

Impact: Multiple production NotePulse customers experienced missing final paragraphs in ~0.8% of long-running streamed responses when using multiplexed sessions behind their in-house reverse proxy. This causes truncated content in user-facing summaries and triggers downstream validation errors in their ingestion pipeline.

Environment: Production, dedicated tier, us-east region. Affected clients are using NotePulse`s multiplexed SSE implementation over a corporate proxy that performs connection pooling and aggressive keepalive trimming.

Observed behavior: In affected sessions the token stream contains all earlier chunks but the last semantic paragraph (2-5 sentences) is replaced by either a heartbeat-only event or is missing entirely. Client receives final keepalive followed by stream close with no explicit end-marker event. Reproduces more frequently when the response is long (>800 tokens) and server send interval overlaps with keepalive schedule.

Expected behavior: Final payload chunk should be delivered, end-marker emitted, then keepalive heartbeat may follow as separate non-interfering frame. Heartbeat traffic should never obscure terminal payloads or end-of-stream metadata.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Use multiplexed SSE session with two concurrent streams on the same connection.
2) Configure server to stream a long-form response (800-1400 tokens) with periodic event-chunking (approx every 200-400ms).
3) Place a reverse proxy in front that applies aggressive connection pooling and issues periodic keepalive probes on the upstream (simulate customer proxy behavior).
4) Observe token stream assembly on client; repeat under high concurrency (50+ concurrent connections) to increase chance of timing overlap.
logs: 2025-02-12T16:04:32.847Z - stream_id=abc123 - CHUNK event: {choice: '...last sentence fragment', meta: {...}}
client SDK trace: assembleChunks(): final_marker not seen, assembled_text ends at '...last sentence fragment'
comments: Elena Park (Support) 2025-02-14: Customer reports ~0.8% failure rate across long responses; provided sample session ids and a minimal repro proxy config. Customer asking for mitigation while we investigate.

Miguel Torres (SRE) 2025-02-15: I reproduced locally using our proxy harness. When a keepalive frame (0-length event) races the final payload chunk, the mux layer occasionally increments the heartbeat stream priority and the client SDK drops trailing payload assembly. Attaching packet capture to internal ticket.

Miguel Torres (SRE) 2025-02-16: Hypothesis: multiplex scheduler treats heartbeat frames as control frames with preemptive ordering; under certain interleavings heartbeat is forwarded before final application chunk and client parser treats subsequent end-marker as lost due to upstream RST.

Elena Park (Support) 2025-02-17: Customer confirmed workaround trial where they increased server final-chunk repetition (send final fragment twice) and saw immediate reduction in incidence. They requested a server-side change rather than client workarounds.
investigation_notes: - Reproduced in internal harness with Nginx reverse-proxy configured to send TCP keepalives at 200ms intervals.
- Packet captures show ordering: final-chunk -> heartbeat -> RST (proxy), but server-to-client muxing may tag heartbeat with higher stream-priority causing client callback to finalize earlier.
- Client SDK (v1.12.3) parser logic: treats keepalive event as 'session control' and emits onControl() which has side-effect of resetting pending terminal-assembly buffer in ~0.5% race cases.
- Serving runtime logs show no exception; the runtime emitted end-marker but it was batched into the same TCP packet as the heartbeat in some cases and proxy split changed framing.
root_cause: Race between mux-level heartbeat prioritization and client-side terminal-assembly logic combined with proxy-induced packet framing changes. Heartbeat control frames were being elevated above concluding payload chunks in the mux scheduler, causing client parser to commit a partial assembly before the explicit end-marker was processed.
resolution_notes: Short-term mitigation: Advise customer to enable server-side final-chunk duplication (server sends concluding fragment twice) or configure proxy to relax keepalive frequency. Customer already applied duplication and reported drop in failure rate.

Medium-term fix: Change mux scheduler to ensure application payload chunks are always delivered before keepalive/control frames when they belong to the same logical stream and final-marker is pending. Also add a client SDK patch to treat heartbeats as non-destructive to pending terminal buffers.
Planned code changes: runtime PR to adjust frame ordering heuristics (runtime PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1892), client SDK PR to update parser commit semantics (sdk PR queued).

Rollout plan: Release runtime patch as canary to Staging on 2025-02-25, monitor stream integrity metrics, then promote to Prod 2025-03-03 behind a controlled rollout. Client SDK patch to be released as v1.12.4 and recommended to Dedicated customers.
resolution_status: Fix in progress: workaround accepted by customer; runtime patch and SDK change in development.
notes_for_followup: - Add an automated regression test that simulates heartbeat/terminal chunk races with several proxy framing variations.
- Create dashboard alert for sudden spikes in 'missing_final_marker' for dedicated customers in us-east.
- Notify Solutions Eng to include best-practice proxy config in Dedicated onboarding docs.
- After production rollout, follow up with NotePulse for a post-deployment validation window (48 hours).
